hero.lede.value: Temple gates before the crowds, maple valleys at their peak, and a last night in a machiya townhouse — one week with a guide who grew up in these streets.

hero.caption.value: Kiyomizu-dera, the temple the city was built around.

highlights.lede.value: Four places set the shape of the week. Everything else hangs off them.

highlights.1.body.value: Ten thousand vermilion gates climb a mountain. We start at 06:00, before the first bus arrives, and walk it upward while it is still silent.

highlights.2.body.value: A windless day in Arashiyama still moves — the whole canopy knocks overhead. We go late afternoon, then tea at a teahouse at the edge of the grove.

highlights.3.body.value: Two of its three storeys are covered in gold leaf, and the pond was designed to give the building a second, steadier copy.

highlights.4.body.value: The lanterns come on around 17:40 and the teahouse lanes change character completely. We walk them slowly, and then eat.

itinerary.lede.value: Each morning is planned; each afternoon leaves room. Nothing starts before the group has had coffee.

itinerary.1.body.value: Meet at Kyoto Station, drop bags, then walk the old south side. Easy evening — Hirano shrine, and dinner wherever the group feels like stopping.

itinerary.2.body.value: Ninenzaka and Sannenzaka before the shops open, Kiyomizu-dera from the rear approach, then down to Gion for the evening walk.

itinerary.3.body.value: The full climb while the gates are empty. Afternoon at leisure — the museum row, or a second attempt on the mountain if your legs allow.

itinerary.4.body.value: Kinkaku-ji early, then Ryoan-ji's fifteen stones and the Nyojindō pavilion. This is the day the guide explains what a garden is actually doing.

itinerary.5.body.value: Tenryū-ji garden in the morning, the grove and Okochi villa after, a boat down the Hozugawa if the water is high enough.

itinerary.6.title.value: Day trip, and a ryokan night

itinerary.6.body.value: Train to Nara for the hall at Tōdai-ji, back by late afternoon, then north into the Higashiyama hills — the machiya, and kaiseki dinner served in your room.

itinerary.7.body.value: Ginkaku-ji's moss garden first thing, the Nishiki market for anything you want to take home, and the station by two o'clock.

reviews.1.body.value: The 06:00 Inari start is the single best decision I have ever taken on a trip. I was alone on the mountain for an hour, and by the time the tour buses came up I was already back in town eating breakfast.

reviews.2.body.value: Seven days sounds long until you realise how much of it is the same four streets, and they are all different every time. Our guide never once read from a phone.

reviews.3.body.value: The ryokan night is the highlight and also the tightest logistics — we arrived later than the schedule said. Worth the wait, but I would build in an extra hour.

booking.lede.value: Eight places per departure, held in booking order. A ¥30,000 deposit secures one; the balance is due sixty days before arrival.

booking.fineprint.value: No payment is taken here. We reply within two working days.

faq.1.a.value: Between six and nine kilometres a day, most of it on flat paved lane. Day three includes the Inari climb — about four hundred metres of steady steps, and you can stop at the Yotsutsuji viewpoint halfway instead of continuing.

faq.2.q.value: Is the April departure before the maple colour?

faq.2.a.value: Yes. April is cherry blossom, not momiji. The maple photographs on this page are from the November departure. If maples are the reason you are coming, book November 8.

faq.3.q.value: What is included in the price?

faq.3.a.value: Seven nights' accommodation, all temple and garden admissions, guiding, and dinner on six of the seven evenings. International flights, travel insurance and lunch are not included.

faq.4.a.value: Roughly half of each group travels alone. Solo travellers share a twin room and pay the listed price; a private room is an extra ¥34,000 for the week.
